chapter: Stories of players and the sister
title: Leon Rappolo and recording at the Bucktown roadhouse
summary: His sister question turns into Bucktown band, declined free record, and Johnny's clarinet.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Did your sister ever make any records by the way? Lucille you mean? Yes.

Yeah, Bernie, no. You see, the first time when I was working out of the Bugtown, Leon Rapport was playing out there, and George E. Brunus, Joe Gowler was playing piano, myself. We used to have corner players. We never had any corner players. We used to have corner players just come in and sit in, you know, like Johnny Lala, Manny Blessie, Paul Merez, and a few guys. We only had trombone, clown and piano and drums, you know. That was one of the jobs, I mean, they really, it was supposed to be a union job and they wasn't any local either. In them days you could, if you couldn't get the union, you know, if you couldn't get anybody in union to play, you could get permission to use. Well anyway, one night out there we were playing and some fella used to come out there every night and listen to the band. One night he said to Leon Rapport, he said, say, man, I'd like to record the band, make a record of it. So Leon came to me this night and he said to me, say, how? He said, no money, no, you know, free alley. And I never played free alley at all. I'd have told my dad I'd make a record for free. So I told him, I said, he said, all you got to bring is a wood block and assemble. He said, well Rapport, you know, I said, I'm not that kind, I'm not a wood blocker. I said, you could get any of these guys that play wood boxers. I said, I'm a, I play on the side of the cell. I said, I'm a drummer. He said, so he wouldn't make the record, see. And him and I used to play the slot machine, we used to call it cow, we'd put in maybe about fifteen, twenty cents a piece of great liquor machine. And man, he wouldn't talk to me for quite a while about that. He was moody, wouldn't talk to me. So one night he said to me, he said, how? He said, let's play cow. First time he even said anything. So we put in maybe fifteen, twenty cents. And we hit the jackpot. And then, every now and then I can see him, counting them nickels, see. He had a hat there, and the money, he had that money and all in the hat, and he stood on the bench, and he was counting the nickels like that, putting them in the box. This is yours, this is mine, this is yours, this is mine. Maybe five hours we wanted, something like that. But yeah, he was a great client, I think. There's no question about that. He was one of the best, better ones that I heard. But Bill Krieger played great. I can't take anything away from him. I think he was one of the great clients then too. Of course there's other guys played. Johnny Provincana played pretty good client there. You never did hear Johnny. Never.

In fact, Johnny used to come out when I worked out at the peak in Inman. Johnny used to come out every now and then play, you know, client. But he played good client there too. Johnny played real good.
